full_title: LAPUY BATTALION EMPLOYEES AGRARIAN REFORM BENEFICIARIES COOPERATIVE (LABEARBCO), REPRESENTED BY ITS CHAIRMAN, MARCOS ENDRINA, PETITIONER, VS. ENRICA O. BABAO, JULIUS ANTONIUS BABAO CO, MARIA ROSALIE BABAO CO, MARIA CONCEPTION BABAO CO, JOSEPHINE BABAO CO, MARIA ELENA BABAO CO, ANTHONY CRIS CO, ENRICO TAJANLANGIT, ANA RICA C. CACHO, MAR VINCE EMMANUEL C. REYES, AND JOHN LEE VINCENT C. REYES, RESPONDENTS.
subject: Remedial Law, Legal and Judicial Ethics
syllabus_topic: III. Civil Procedure > T. Execution, Satisfaction, and Effect of Judgments (Rule 39) > 7. Effect of Judgments or Final Orders
topics: A judgment binds only the parties; no execution against non-parties
Treating a new case as a mere motion to execute an old judgment
Collateral attack on a Torrens title (Sec. 48, PD 1529)
Grave abuse of discretion by an agrarian adjudicator

other_subjects.subject: Civil Law and Land Titles and Deeds
other_subjects.syllabus_topic: VI. Land Titles and Deeds (PD 1529, as amended by RA 6732 and 11573) > F. Certificate of Title

other_subjects.subject: Political and Public International Law
other_subjects.syllabus_topic: VIII. Constitutional Rights > A. Due Process > 2. Judicial and Administrative Due Process

doctrine:
**A person cannot be prejudiced by a ruling in a case to which he was not made a party. A writ of execution may be issued only against a party, not against one who did not have his day in court** (*Green Acres Holdings v. Cabral*). This principle conforms to the constitutional guarantee of due process. An adjudicator gravely abuses its discretion when it consolidates a new case against holders of derivative titles with an old, final case and orders the old judgment implemented against them, instead of deciding the new case on the merits. Doing so treats the new case as a mere motion for execution and binds the titleholders without a hearing.

**A Torrens title cannot be altered, modified or cancelled except in a direct proceeding (Sec. 48, PD 1529).** An attack is direct when the object of the action is to annul or set aside the title, and collateral when it is made as an incident in an action for a different relief (*Hortizuela v. Tagufa*). Cancelling the derivative titles of persons who were not impleaded, by implementing a judgment that only annulled an extrajudicial settlement of estate, is a prohibited collateral attack. The Court agreed with the CA that the agrarian adjudicator (RARAD) had no jurisdiction to entertain the action for cancellation of certificates of title issued to third persons. Reiterated.
facts:
Manuel P. Babao was the registered owner of two parcels in Lapuy, Tigatto, Davao City: TCT No. T-1460 (413,439 sq m) and TCT No. T-561 (210,025 sq m). When he died on July 10, 1984, the lands passed to his wife, Rosa Ong Chua, and daughter, Enrica. In 1989 the DAR notified Chua that the lands would be covered by CARP, and she obtained a 10-year deferment that expired on June 15, 1998. Chua died on June 10, 1996, leaving Enrica as sole heir. After the deferment expired, the DAR issued new Notices of Coverage for both titles in 1998. On March 3, 1999, Enrica executed a Deed of Extrajudicial Settlement of Manuel's estate, adjudicating the lands to herself and her children.

The DAR sued before the Provincial Agrarian Reform Adjudicator (PARAD) to annul the extrajudicial settlement (DARAB Case No. XI-1783-DC-2003, the 2003 case). Enrica et al. questioned the DARAB's jurisdiction. On September 5, 2003, the PARAD declared the settlement void and directed the Register of Deeds to reinstate the two TCTs in Manuel's name and cancel all derivative titles. No appeal was taken, and the decision became final.

The Register of Deeds did not act on the writ of execution because it was uncertain which titles to cancel. On May 22, 2008, the PARAD denied the DAR's motion for an alias writ specifying the derivative titles. It held that titles issued to persons who were not parties could not be cancelled without a direct proceeding, and the RARAD denied reconsideration. The DAR then filed DARAB Case No. XI-2057-DC-2008 (the 2008 case) to cancel the derivative titles. It impleaded Enrica et al., several other titleholders (Jaime Babado, Gunie B. Cornelio, Gloriosa Vicera, Gerino Macrohon, Manuel Co, Jesus Enrie Co and Lorenzo T. Ng), and the Register of Deeds.

On January 12, 2011, the RARAD consolidated the 2003 and 2008 cases and directed the implementation of the September 5, 2003 decision. On February 14, 2011, it denied Enrica et al.'s notice of appeal because they had not furnished the DARAB a copy, and on March 22, 2011 it denied their omnibus motion. On certiorari, the CA (December 11, 2013) annulled the three Orders. It held that the RARAD had treated the 2008 case as a mere motion for execution and nullified the derivative titles without hearing respondents who were not impleaded in the 2003 case. It also held that the RARAD had no jurisdiction to annul those titles in what amounted to a collateral attack. The CA denied reconsideration on September 23, 2014. LABEARBCO, an agrarian reform beneficiaries' cooperative, filed a Rule 45 petition.
issues: Whether the RARAD gravely abused its discretion in consolidating the 2008 case with the 2003 case and ordering the 2003 PARAD Decision implemented against the derivative titles, without hearing titleholders who were not parties to the 2003 case.
Whether cancelling the derivative titles in this manner was a collateral attack on the titles, beyond the RARAD's jurisdiction.
ruling:
**1. Yes.** Grave abuse of discretion is a capricious and whimsical exercise of judgment equivalent to lack of jurisdiction, so patent and gross as to amount to an evasion of a positive duty (*Pascual v. Burgos*). The RARAD consolidated the cases, ordered the 2003 decision implemented, and declared the derivative titles void, all without giving the respondents in the 2008 case who were not impleaded in the 2003 case a chance to be heard. It "treated the second case as a mere motion to implement" the 2003 decision. This violated the due process principle that a person cannot be prejudiced by a ruling in a proceeding to which he was not a party. Strangers to a case are not bound by the judgment, and a writ of execution may issue only against a party (*Green Acres*). The CA correctly found grave abuse of discretion.

**2. Yes.** Under *Hortizuela v. Tagufa*, a Torrens title may be cancelled only in a direct proceeding. The 2003 case sought only the annulment of the extrajudicial settlement. The PARAD itself had refused an alias writ because the derivative titles of non-parties could not be cancelled without a direct proceeding, which is why the DAR filed the 2008 case. Yet instead of deciding the 2008 case on the merits, the RARAD used the 2003 decision to annul the derivative titles of persons never impleaded in it. **This was a collateral attack, because the relief sought in the 2003 case was the annulment of the extrajudicial settlement, not the cancellation of those titles.** The RARAD thus gravely abused its discretion, and the Court agreed with the CA that it had no jurisdiction to entertain the action for cancellation of certificates of title issued to third persons.
disposition: The Petition for Review on Certiorari was DENIED. The CA's December 11, 2013 Decision and September 23, 2014 Resolution in CA-G.R. SP No. 04191-MIN, which annulled and set aside the RARAD's Orders of January 12, February 14 and March 22, 2011, were AFFIRMED.

bar_questions.q: In a final judgment, the RTC annulled a deed of extrajudicial settlement executed by Ana and her children. It ordered the Register of Deeds to reinstate the mother title in the decedent's name and to cancel "all derivative titles." Before the suit, Ana's son had sold portions of the land to Ben and Carmen, who obtained their own TCTs. Ben and Carmen were never impleaded. The winning party now moves for an alias writ of execution directing the cancellation of Ben's and Carmen's titles. Should the motion be granted?

alac.answer: No. The judgment cannot be executed against Ben and Carmen, and their titles cannot be cancelled this way.
alac.legal_basis: A person cannot be prejudiced by a ruling in an action to which he was not made a party, and a writ of execution may issue only against a party, not against one who did not have his day in court. Under Section 48 of PD 1529, a certificate of title cannot be altered, modified or cancelled except in a direct proceeding; an attack made as an incident of an action for a different relief is collateral. (LABEARBCO v. Babao, G.R. No. 215129, September 29, 2025)
alac.application: Ben and Carmen were strangers to the annulment case and were never heard, so the judgment does not bind them. The object of that case was to annul the extrajudicial settlement, not to cancel their titles, so cancelling their titles through an alias writ would be a collateral attack. The winning party must file a direct action to annul their titles, impleading them.
alac.conclusion: The motion for an alias writ should be denied as to Ben's and Carmen's titles.

bar_questions.q: After the alias writ was denied, the winning party filed a separate complaint before the RTC to annul Ben's and Carmen's titles, impleading both. (a) Ben moves to dismiss, arguing that the complaint is a prohibited collateral attack on his Torrens title. Is he correct? (b) Suppose the court, instead of trying the new case, consolidates it with the old annulment case and, without hearing Ben and Carmen, orders the old judgment implemented to cancel their titles. Is that order valid?

alac.answer: (a) No. The new complaint is a direct attack on the titles. (b) No. The order is a grave abuse of discretion because it binds non-parties without a hearing and cancels their titles collaterally.
alac.legal_basis: An attack on a title is direct when the object of the action is to annul or set it aside, and collateral when it is made as an incident of an action for a different relief (Sec. 48, PD 1529; Hortizuela v. Tagufa). A tribunal that consolidates a new case against titleholders with an old, final case and orders the old judgment implemented against them, treating the new case as a mere motion for execution without hearing them, gravely abuses its discretion. (LABEARBCO v. Babao, G.R. No. 215129, September 29, 2025)
alac.application: (a) The sole object of the new complaint is to annul Ben's and Carmen's titles, and both are impleaded, so it is the direct proceeding Section 48 requires. (b) Consolidating the new case with the old one and simply implementing the old judgment is exactly what the RARAD did in LABEARBCO. It denies Ben and Carmen their day in court and cancels their titles through a judgment that sought a different relief.
alac.conclusion: Ben's motion to dismiss should be denied, but the court must decide the new case on the merits after hearing Ben and Carmen; an order simply implementing the old judgment against them is void for grave abuse of discretion.

bar_questions.q: An agrarian adjudicator ordered a final decision annulling a deed of extrajudicial settlement to be implemented by cancelling the titles of Dario, who bought part of the land and was never a party to that case. Dario was not given notice or a hearing. Dario filed a petition for certiorari with the Court of Appeals, invoking due process. The cooperative that benefits from the order argues that executing a final and executory decision is a ministerial duty, so there can be no grave abuse of discretion. Who is correct?

alac.answer: Dario is correct. The adjudicator gravely abused its discretion and violated his right to due process.
alac.legal_basis: Grave abuse of discretion is a capricious and whimsical exercise of judgment equivalent to lack of jurisdiction, so patent and gross as to amount to an evasion of a positive duty (Pascual v. Burgos). The principle that a person cannot be prejudiced by a ruling in a proceeding to which he was not a party conforms to the constitutional guarantee of due process (Const., Art. III, Sec. 1). Strangers to a case are not bound by the judgment, and a writ of execution may issue only against a party. (LABEARBCO v. Babao, G.R. No. 215129, September 29, 2025)
alac.application: Whatever ministerial character execution has extends only to the parties bound by the judgment. Dario was a stranger to the annulment case, so the final decision cannot be enforced against him. Cancelling his title without notice or hearing deprives him of property without due process, and doing so through a decision that granted a different relief is a collateral attack on his title. That is an arbitrary exercise of power amounting to grave abuse of discretion.
alac.conclusion: The adjudicator's order should be annulled on certiorari for grave abuse of discretion.

notes:
First Division. Hernando, J. (Acting Chairperson), Zalameda and Marquez, JJ. concurred; Gesmundo, C.J. was on official leave. The Court did not separately address two of the petitioner's arguments. The first was that the notice of appeal was properly denied under Rule XIV, Section 1 of the 2003 DARAB Rules (failure to furnish the DARAB a copy). The second was that the CA should not have set aside the January 12, 2011 Order, which was not assailed. The affirmance rests on the grave abuse of discretion found.

The text has apparent typographical errors. It refers several times to a "September 5, 2023" decision; the PARAD Decision is dated September 5, 2003. The quoted *Hortizuela* passage cites "P.D. No. 1528" for PD 1529. The discussion ends by declaring "all proceedings rendered in DARAB Case No. XI-1783-DC-2003" void, although it concerns the RARAD's orders in the 2008 case (DARAB Case No. XI-2057-DC-2008); the fallo only affirms the CA. The decision does not explain how LABEARBCO became a party.
